claims.text: Multicomponent high-entropy alloys are typically nearly equiatomic, with individual elemental concentrations in the 5–35 at.% range.
The applicable systems include both solid and liquid high-entropy alloys at approximately 0.95–1.05 Tm.
A machine-learning interatomic potential should be trained on ab initio configurations spanning both high-temperature solid and liquid phases.
Neural-network or Gaussian-approximation potentials can represent the diverse many-body configurational landscape of high-temperature HEAs.
Conventional EAM methods show clear deficiencies for near-melting solid and liquid HEAs.
A trained MLIP can accurately reproduce the many-body potential-energy surface of the ab initio HEA system.
Accurate reproduction of the ab initio potential-energy surface will make the MLIP ensemble properly represent liquid and solid atomic configurations.
Sampling the full spectrum of high-temperature HEA atomic environments in training enables an MLIP to capture subtle many-body interactions and configurational effects.
Traditional EAM potentials miss subtle many-body interactions and configurational effects present in high-temperature HEAs.
The presence of multiple elements and differing atomic sizes produces lattice distortions and variations in local atomic environments in high-entropy alloys.
Greater MLIP fidelity will improve phase-space overlap between the reference and ab initio target ensembles.
Improved reference–target phase-space overlap will reduce discrepancies along the thermodynamic-integration path.
The MLIP reference will reduce TI path mismatch by at least 50% relative to TOR-TILD EAM references.
The MLIP approach will achieve a free-energy error of approximately 5 meV/atom relative to full ab initio calculations.
TOR-TILD EAM references inadequately sample the diverse configurational space of the ab initio liquid and consequently produce larger TI path mismatches.
The expected improvement is limited to high-melting, near-equiatomic multicomponent HEAs around 0.95–1.05 Tm.
Outside the specified composition or temperature range, the MLIP may require retraining and may not retain the claimed TI improvement.
Elemental and binary calculations provide promising evidence for the flexibility and accuracy of MLIPs.
MLIP transferability across the full HEA composition space and to conditions outside the training range remains uncertain.
Failure to reduce TI path mismatch by at least 50%, or a remaining free-energy error above approximately 5 meV/atom, would falsify the hypothesis.
